screens.title: Implementing Push Notifications
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll demystify push notifications for React Native apps and focus on practical steps you can use right away. You will learn the difference between local notifications—those scheduled by the app on the device—and remote notifications sent from a backend through APNS, FCM, or Expo's push service. We'll cover the crucial permission flow that mobile platforms require, how to obtain and safely send device tokens to your server, and the lifecycle of tokens which can change or expire. You'll see a complete local-notification flow, learn to register listeners for receipt and user taps, and learn when to prefer local scheduling versus a server-triggered remote message. We'll also emphasize platform considerations: Android notification channels and iOS push capability configuration for bare projects, and the practical need to test on a physical device. By the end you will understand what part runs on the device, what belongs on the server, and how to avoid common mistakes like ignoring permission checks or failing to update tokens. Ready to explore scheduling, permissions, and token management in code and design a reminder workflow you can test on your phone?

screens.title: Local vs Remote Notifications
screens.narratorSegment: Let's clarify the difference between local and remote notifications and why the distinction matters for architecture and delivery. Local notifications are scheduled by the app on the device. They are ideal for reminders, timers, and alarms that depend only on local state. Because they don't require a backend, they are easier to implement and often more reliable for client-side deadlines. A concrete example: schedule a follow-up reminder two hours after a user adds an item to a cart; the app can schedule a local notification to fire at that time without contacting a server. Remote notifications are sent from a server through a push service like APNS, FCM, or Expo Push Service. Use remote messages when the server decides timing or when you need to inform many devices simultaneously, such as a flash sale. For instance, your backend triggers a remote notification to notify all users about a time-limited offer. A common misconception is that local notifications are always private; they can still expose data in the notification body so avoid including sensitive information. Key takeaway: prefer local scheduling for single-device timers and remote notifications for server-timed or broadcast events. Consider token management and permissions when choosing either approach.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Local vs Remote Notifications
Local Notifications (Definition)
Scheduled by the app on the device. No server required. Good for reminders, alarms, and client-side timers.
• Example: Schedule a reminder two hours after an item is added to a cart.
• Misconception: Local means private — avoid including sensitive data in notification text.
Remote Notifications (Definition)
Sent from a backend via APNS, FCM, or Expo. Used for broadcasts, server-scheduled events, or when content is generated server-side.
• Example: Send a flash sale alert to segmented users at a fixed time.
• Misconception: Remote guarantees delivery — networks, token invalidation, or misconfigured payloads can cause failures.
Decision Matrix
When device alone decides (use local)
When server decides timing or broadcast (use remote)
Key factors: timing origin, audience size, data sensitivity, need for server coordination, and device connectivity.
Key Takeaway
Choose local for client timers and remote for server-driven broadcasts. Manage permissions and tokens in both paths.

screens.title: Permissions Flow and Fallbacks
screens.narratorSegment: Permissions are the gatekeeper for notifications. The correct flow is: check current permissions, request if not already granted, and handle the result with clear user guidance. Start by calling getPermissionsAsync to read the current status. If the status isn't granted, call requestPermissionsAsync to open the system prompt. On iOS this presents a prominent system dialog; on Android many versions allow notifications without explicit consent, but some versions and features require user approval. Always design a fallback UX: if the user denies permission, explain why notifications add value and provide an in-app path that opens the device settings so they can re-enable permissions. A practical example: when a user opts-in to reminders, show a short modal describing how reminders improve their experience, then call requestPermissionsAsync. If denied, show a persistent opt-in card with an explanation and a link to settings. A common mistake is attempting to schedule or fetch tokens before permission is granted — this leads to silent failures. Key takeaway: treat permission checks as a first-class UX step and handle denial with clear value propositions and a guided path to settings.

keyIdea.title: Permission pattern
keyIdea.text: Check permissions first, request if needed, and provide a clear fallback if the user denies access.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Permissions Flow and Fallbacks
Permission Steps
  1. Call getPermissionsAsync to inspect existing status.
  2. If not granted, call requestPermissionsAsync to prompt the user.
  3. If denied, show an explanation and guide to device settings.
  4. Only after granted, obtain tokens and schedule notifications.
Important: do not schedule notifications or request a token before permission is granted. This causes silent failures and poor UX.
Example check and request (pseudocode)
const { status: existing } = await Notifications.getPermissionsAsync()
let finalStatus = existing
if (existing !== 'granted') {
  const { status } = await Notifications.requestPermissionsAsync()
  finalStatus = status
}
if (finalStatus !== 'granted') {
  // show fallback UI and explain benefits
}
UX Patterns for Denial
Show a short explanation of benefits, let the user postpone, and provide a clear path to the device's app settings so they can enable notifications later.
Misconception: prompting repeatedly will increase opt-ins. Repeated intrusive prompts can drive users away. Use contextual explanations before asking.
Key Takeaway
Treat permission as a UX decision. Explain value, check status, request once, and offer settings guidance on denial.

screens.title: Device Tokens and What They Mean
screens.narratorSegment: Device tokens are unique identifiers created by a push service for a given app installation on a device. They are essential because your backend uses these tokens to target specific devices when sending remote notifications. In an Expo managed workflow you obtain an Expo Push Token using getExpoPushTokenAsync; Expo wraps the platform token so the Expo push service can deliver messages. In bare React Native with Firebase you obtain an FCM token. Tokens should be sent to your backend and associated with a user or installation record. Expect tokens to change: tokens can expire, be rotated by the system, or become invalid after app reinstall. Your server must handle updates and invalidations: if a push service returns an error for a token, mark it for refresh and attempt to re-register. Don't leak tokens publicly and do not embed sensitive data in tokens. A concrete example: after a successful registerForPushNotificationsAsync, POST the returned token to your /api/devices endpoint with the current user id. Key takeaway: treat tokens as replacement addresses for devices — keep them secure, up-to-date, and associated with accounts so remote notifications reach the intended recipients.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Device Tokens and What They Mean
What is a device token?
A token is a service-issued identifier for a device and app installation that your backend uses to target notifications.
• Expo Push Token: returned by getExpoPushTokenAsync in managed Expo projects.
• FCM Token: used in bare React Native projects integrating Firebase Cloud Messaging.
• APNS Token: the platform-level token used on iOS behind the scenes.
Practical: after obtaining the token, send it to your backend with the user id. Keep a mapping so you can target devices for remote notifications.
Server-side considerations
Store tokens securely, track their created_at and last_seen, and implement logic to remove tokens that become invalid or return errors from the push service.
Misconception: tokens never change. In reality, tokens can and will change; plan to re-register and update server records when the app restarts or after reinstall.
Key Takeaway
Treat tokens as device addresses. Send them to your server, keep them current, and remove invalid tokens to maintain delivery quality.

screens.title: Registering Tokens and Backend Workflow
screens.narratorSegment: Once you have a device token, the next step is registering it with your backend. The typical workflow begins on the client: after permissions are granted and you obtain an Expo or FCM token, make a secure POST request to your server endpoint with the token and the user's identifier. On the server, validate the token format briefly, associate it with the user's account or installation, and store metadata such as platform, created_at, and last_seen. When sending remote notifications, the server selects tokens for the target users and posts messages to the push service A P I. Implement error handling: if a push service responds that a token is invalid or unregistered, mark it for removal or refresh. Also consider token rotation — when users reinstall or restore devices tokens will change, so update records at app startup or when you detect a token difference. Privacy note: do not expose tokens publicly, and avoid storing sensitive user data in tokens. A concrete example: client sends POST /api/devices { userId, token, platform } and the server saves it; later the server uses that record to call the Expo push A P I with the token. Key takeaway: build robust server logic that accepts tokens, verifies delivery results, and removes or refreshes invalid tokens.

keyIdea.title: Backend steps
keyIdea.text: Client obtains token and securely sends it to the backend; server records and uses it to call push service APIs and must handle invalidations.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Registering Tokens and Backend Workflow
Client → Server → Push Service
Sequence: obtain token on client, POST to your backend, backend stores token and later sends to push service API to deliver messages.
• Client POST: /api/devices { userId, token, platform }
• Server: store token with metadata, run delivery and error handling.
• On push failure: mark token invalid and prompt client to re-register next app launch.
Example payload to backend (JSON)
{
  "userId": "user-123",
  "platform": "android",
  "token": "ExpoPushToken[xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx]"
}
Error Handling
If the push service returns 'InvalidToken' or 'NotRegistered', mark the record and attempt to refresh the token on next app run. Keep metrics for delivery success and failures.
Key Takeaway
Your server is responsible for storing tokens, sending messages, and handling failures. Design for token rotation and invalidation.

screens.title: Scheduling Local Notifications
screens.narratorSegment: Now we'll walk through a concrete local-notification example that schedules a reminder. The key A P I is scheduleNotificationAsync which accepts a content object and a trigger. The content carries title, body, and an optional data object. The trigger can be a simple seconds delay or a calendar trigger. In the chapter example we schedule a notification to fire after two seconds to demonstrate behavior quickly. Always ensure permissions are granted before scheduling; otherwise scheduleNotificationAsync may fail silently. A practical example: scheduleNotificationAsync({ content: { title: "You've got mail!", body: 'Here is the notification body', data: { someData: 'goes here' } }, trigger: { seconds: 2 } }). Use setNotificationHandler to define how notifications appear while the app is foregrounded; for instance you might show an alert but disable sound or badges. A common mistake is leaving heavy work in the notification body; instead include small data keys and fetch secure content when the user opens the app. Key takeaway: schedule small, actionable notifications and use data payloads to fetch protected content after the app opens. Scheduling Local Notifications means use schedulenotificationasync with content and trigger, and ensure permissions are granted before calling.. In practical terms, using schedulenotificationasync to create reminders. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Scheduling Local Notifications
Set notification handler
Notifications.setNotificationHandler({
  handleNotification: async () => ({
    shouldShowAlert: true,
    shouldPlaySound: false,
    shouldSetBadge: false,
  }),
})
Schedule example
await Notifications.scheduleNotificationAsync({
  content: {
    title: "You've got mail! 📬",
    body: 'Here is the notification body',
    data: { someData: 'goes here' },
  },
  trigger: { seconds: 2 },
})
Tip: Keep notification bodies short and include a small data payload for secure fetch after the app opens.
Example scenario
User sets a reminder message and delay. After confirming permission, call scheduleNotificationAsync to show the reminder at the requested time.
Key Takeaway
Use scheduleNotificationAsync for local reminders and setNotificationHandler to control foreground presentation.

screens.title: Listening for Notifications and User Response
screens.narratorSegment: To make notifications useful you must listen for them and respond to user interactions. expo-notifications offers two important listeners. addNotificationReceivedListener fires when a notification arrives while the app is in the foreground. You can use this to update UI state or show an in-app banner. addNotificationResponseReceivedListener fires when a user taps or interacts with a notification, regardless of whether the app was foregrounded, backgrounded, or killed. This listener provides the notification request and any data payload so you can deep-link to specific content. In practice, register both listeners inside a useEffect and store their subscriptions so you can remove them on unmount. A concrete example from the chapter logs the response and shows an alert when tapped. Also handle edge cases: when the app is launched from a killed state via a notification, ensure initial notification data is processed so navigation occurs only once. Common mistake: forgetting to remove subscriptions on cleanup which can lead to duplicates in long-lived sessions. Key takeaway: register both listeners to create responsive, context-aware notification behavior and always clean up subscriptions. Listening for Notifications and User Response means use addnotificationreceivedlistener to react to arrivals, and addnotificationresponsereceivedlistener to handle taps and deep links.. In practical terms, addnotificationreceivedlistener and addnotificationresponsereceivedlistener. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Listening for Notifications and User Response
Listener example
// notification received while app is foregrounded
notificationListener.current = Notifications.addNotificationReceivedListener(notification => {
  setNotification(notification)
})

// notification tapped by user
responseListener.current = Notifications.addNotificationResponseReceivedListener(response => {
  // use response.notification.request.content.data to deep-link
})
Remember to store subscriptions in refs and remove them in cleanup to prevent duplicate handlers.
Handling app launch from notification
If the app is started by a notification tap, check the initial notification or response to route the user to the appropriate screen once.
Common Mistake
Not removing listeners on unmount, causing multiple triggers over time. Always clean up subscriptions.

screens.title: Android Notification Channels
screens.narratorSegment: Notification channels let Android users control notification behavior by category: sound, vibration, importance, and light. For apps targeting Android, creating channels is essential to ensure your notifications appear with the intended behavior and that users have granular control. Use Notifications. setNotificationChannelAsync to create a channel with a name, importance level, vibration pattern, and light color. For example, you might create a 'reminders' channel with high importance and brief vibration, and a 'news' channel with default importance. A common pitfall is forgetting to create channels on Android; without them notifications may fall back to default behavior or be suppressed on some devices. Another important point: channels are persistent on the device. If you change a channel's settings in code, users may have adjusted that channel, so updating channel metadata won't override a user's custom settings. Practical advice: create channels at app startup or during an onboarding flow, and clearly label each channel so users understand what they control. Key takeaway: channels are the Android mechanism for letting users tune notification behavior per category; configure them intentionally before delivering notifications. screens.title: Remote Notification Delivery Flow
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the remote delivery flow helps you diagnose problems and design reliable systems. The flow begins when your server decides to send a notification. The server constructs a payload and targets tokens stored for users, then sends the payload to the push service: APNS for iOS, FCM for Android, or Expo Push Service when using Expo tokens. The push service validates the token, authenticates the request, and enqueues delivery to the device's OS. The OS then delivers the notification to the device. If delivery fails because a token is invalid, the push service returns an error to your server. Your server should log failures and remove or mark tokens for refresh. For high-volume apps, batch and rate-limit requests and handle responses asynchronously. A common misconception is that the server alone guarantees delivery; network issues, token invalidation, or user settings can block notifications. A concrete example: your backend triggers a flash sale notification, posts to the Expo Push A P I with numerous Expo Push Tokens, and processes responses to remove tokens flagged as invalid. Key takeaway: build server workflows that send, monitor, and reconcile push delivery feedback to keep token lists healthy and reliable.

screens.title: Reminder App Walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity guides you through building a simple reminder app that schedules local notifications and handles taps. screens.title: Common Mistakes and Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: When implementing notifications you will encounter recurring issues. First, permission denials: failing to check permissions before scheduling or fetching a token often causes silent failures. Always call getPermissionsAsync and handle 'denied' with a clear fallback. Second, simulators often do not fully support push behavior; testing on a physical device is essential to validate tokens and remote delivery. Third, token management mistakes: failing to update tokens after reinstall or ignoring push service error responses will cause delivery to break. Implement server-side logic to remove invalid tokens and re-register tokens at app startup. Fourth, misconfigured payloads: push services have specific payload shapes; sending the wrong fields or an unsupported type can lead to rejected messages. For Android, neglecting channels can result in unexpected silent behavior. Finally, privacy and spam: sending too many or irrelevant notifications causes users to disable notifications or uninstall the app. A concrete troubleshooting step: if remote notifications aren't arriving, verify permission status, confirm token registration on the server, check the server response from the push service, and ensure the device is reachable. Key takeaway: combine permission checks, device testing, token lifecycle handling, and careful payload construction to avoid most issues.

screens.title: Privacy, Frequency, and Content Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Notifications touch user attention and trust, so privacy and prudent delivery matter. Only send notifications that are relevant and actionable. Avoid placing sensitive data in notification bodies because notifications may be visible on locked screens and are not always encrypted in transit. Instead include an identifier or small data payload and fetch secure content when the user opens the app. Limit frequency: define sensible cadence rules and user preferences so users can opt out of categories they don't want. Provide in-app controls and clearly labeled channels on Android so users can control behavior. For security, transmit tokens over HTTPS, store them securely on your backend, and avoid logging tokens in places accessible to other services. Consider adding server-side throttling and deduplication so users don't receive repeated messages for the same event. A practical policy: include a settings screen where users can toggle reminder categories, and honor these preferences before scheduling local alarms or sending remote pushes. Key takeaway: treat notifications as a privilege — be transparent, minimize sensitive content, and provide meaningful controls to retain trust. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll demystify push notifications for React Native apps and focus on practical steps you can use right away. You will learn the difference between local notifications—those scheduled by the app on the device—and remote notifications sent from a backend through APNS, FCM, or Expo's push service. We'll cover the crucial permission flow that mobile platforms require, how to obtain and safely send device tokens to your server, and the lifecycle of tokens which can change or expire. You'll see a complete local-notification flow, learn to register listeners for receipt and user taps, and learn when to prefer local scheduling versus a server-triggered remote message. We'll also emphasize platform considerations: Android notification channels and iOS push capability configuration for bare projects, and the practical need to test on a physical device. By the end you will understand what part runs on the device, what belongs on the server, and how to avoid common mistakes like ignoring permission checks or failing to update tokens. Ready to explore scheduling, permissions, and token management in code and design a reminder workflow you can test on your phone?

By the end of this chapter you will have four practical competencies that let you add reliable notifications to a React Native app. First, you will understand notification types and when to use local scheduling versus remote server-triggered messages. This helps you choose the simplest, most robust approach for reminders, alarms, or broadcast events. Second, you'll be able to request and check notification permissions on both iOS and Android and design graceful fallback behavior when users deny access. Protecting the user experience here avoids silent failures and reduces frustration. Third, you'll generate and register device tokens using expo-notifications, and learn how to send those tokens securely to your backend so you can target devices. Finally, you'll schedule and handle local notifications, register listeners for receipt and taps, and test on physical devices. Each skill includes a short mnemonic or visual cue so you can remember the flow: Type → Permission → Token → Handle. These objectives map directly to a verified competency milestone you can demonstrate with the reminder app and a server-side token registration.

This continuation highlights the practical outcomes and how you'll demonstrate competency. You will implement permission requests using the expo-notifications A P I, specifically calling methods to check current status and to prompt the system dialog when needed. You'll learn to interpret status results and to design fallback UX when permissions are denied. Next, you'll implement token retrieval using getExpoPushTokenAsync and understand how that token differs from platform tokens. You will practice sending tokens to your backend and designing server logic that safely stores, rotates, and invalidates tokens when they expire or when delivery fails. You will also add listeners for notification receipt and user response, so the app can update UI or deep-link to content when a user taps a notification. Finally, you will test notification channels on Android and verify iOS capabilities for bare apps. Each step maps to a demonstrable task: schedule a local reminder, retrieve a token and POST it to a test endpoint, and respond to a tapped notification with navigation. These are the actions you will perform to prove your verified competency milestone.

Let's clarify the difference between local and remote notifications and why the distinction matters for architecture and delivery. Local notifications are scheduled by the app on the device. They are ideal for reminders, timers, and alarms that depend only on local state. Because they don't require a backend, they are easier to implement and often more reliable for client-side deadlines. A concrete example: schedule a follow-up reminder two hours after a user adds an item to a cart; the app can schedule a local notification to fire at that time without contacting a server. Remote notifications are sent from a server through a push service like APNS, FCM, or Expo Push Service. Use remote messages when the server decides timing or when you need to inform many devices simultaneously, such as a flash sale. For instance, your backend triggers a remote notification to notify all users about a time-limited offer. A common misconception is that local notifications are always private; they can still expose data in the notification body so avoid including sensitive information. Key takeaway: prefer local scheduling for single-device timers and remote notifications for server-timed or broadcast events. Consider token management and permissions when choosing either approach.

Permissions are the gatekeeper for notifications. The correct flow is: check current permissions, request if not already granted, and handle the result with clear user guidance. Start by calling getPermissionsAsync to read the current status. If the status isn't granted, call requestPermissionsAsync to open the system prompt. On iOS this presents a prominent system dialog; on Android many versions allow notifications without explicit consent, but some versions and features require user approval. Always design a fallback UX: if the user denies permission, explain why notifications add value and provide an in-app path that opens the device settings so they can re-enable permissions. A practical example: when a user opts-in to reminders, show a short modal describing how reminders improve their experience, then call requestPermissionsAsync. If denied, show a persistent opt-in card with an explanation and a link to settings. A common mistake is attempting to schedule or fetch tokens before permission is granted — this leads to silent failures. Key takeaway: treat permission checks as a first-class UX step and handle denial with clear value propositions and a guided path to settings.

Device tokens are unique identifiers created by a push service for a given app installation on a device. They are essential because your backend uses these tokens to target specific devices when sending remote notifications. In an Expo managed workflow you obtain an Expo Push Token using getExpoPushTokenAsync; Expo wraps the platform token so the Expo push service can deliver messages. In bare React Native with Firebase you obtain an FCM token. Tokens should be sent to your backend and associated with a user or installation record. Expect tokens to change: tokens can expire, be rotated by the system, or become invalid after app reinstall. Your server must handle updates and invalidations: if a push service returns an error for a token, mark it for refresh and attempt to re-register. Don't leak tokens publicly and do not embed sensitive data in tokens. A concrete example: after a successful registerForPushNotificationsAsync, POST the returned token to your /api/devices endpoint with the current user id. Key takeaway: treat tokens as replacement addresses for devices — keep them secure, up-to-date, and associated with accounts so remote notifications reach the intended recipients.

Once you have a device token, the next step is registering it with your backend. The typical workflow begins on the client: after permissions are granted and you obtain an Expo or FCM token, make a secure POST request to your server endpoint with the token and the user's identifier. On the server, validate the token format briefly, associate it with the user's account or installation, and store metadata such as platform, created_at, and last_seen. When sending remote notifications, the server selects tokens for the target users and posts messages to the push service A P I. Implement error handling: if a push service responds that a token is invalid or unregistered, mark it for removal or refresh. Also consider token rotation — when users reinstall or restore devices tokens will change, so update records at app startup or when you detect a token difference. Privacy note: do not expose tokens publicly, and avoid storing sensitive user data in tokens. A concrete example: client sends POST /api/devices { userId, token, platform } and the server saves it; later the server uses that record to call the Expo push A P I with the token. Key takeaway: build robust server logic that accepts tokens, verifies delivery results, and removes or refreshes invalid tokens.

Now we'll walk through a concrete local-notification example that schedules a reminder. The key A P I is scheduleNotificationAsync which accepts a content object and a trigger. The content carries title, body, and an optional data object. The trigger can be a simple seconds delay or a calendar trigger. In the chapter example we schedule a notification to fire after two seconds to demonstrate behavior quickly. Always ensure permissions are granted before scheduling; otherwise scheduleNotificationAsync may fail silently. A practical example: scheduleNotificationAsync({ content: { title: "You've got mail!", body: 'Here is the notification body', data: { someData: 'goes here' } }, trigger: { seconds: 2 } }). The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

This listener provides the notification request and any data payload so you can deep-link to specific content. Also handle edge cases: when the app is launched from a killed state via a notification, ensure initial notification data is processed so navigation occurs only once. Understanding the remote delivery flow helps you diagnose problems and design reliable systems. The flow begins when your server decides to send a notification. The server constructs a payload and targets tokens stored for users, then sends the payload to the push service: APNS for iOS, FCM for Android, or Expo Push Service when using Expo tokens. The push service validates the token, authenticates the request, and enqueues delivery to the device's OS. The OS then delivers the notification to the device. If delivery fails because a token is invalid, the push service returns an error to your server. Your server should log failures and remove or mark tokens for refresh. For high-volume apps, batch and rate-limit requests and handle responses asynchronously. A common misconception is that the server alone guarantees delivery; network issues, token invalidation, or user settings can block notifications. A concrete example: your backend triggers a flash sale notification, posts to the Expo Push A P I with numerous Expo Push Tokens, and processes responses to remove tokens flagged as invalid. Key takeaway: build server workflows that send, monitor, and reconcile push delivery feedback to keep token lists healthy and reliable.

When implementing notifications you will encounter recurring issues. First, permission denials: failing to check permissions before scheduling or fetching a token often causes silent failures. Implement server-side logic to remove invalid tokens and re-register tokens at app startup. Fourth, misconfigured payloads: push services have specific payload shapes; sending the wrong fields or an unsupported type can lead to rejected messages. Key takeaway: combine permission checks, device testing, token lifecycle handling, and careful payload construction to avoid most issues.

Let's consolidate the most important takeaways. First, understand the core distinction: local notifications are scheduled on-device and are best for client-side timers; remote notifications come from a backend through APNS, FCM, or Expo and are used for server-driven or broadcast messages. Second, permissions must be checked and requested responsibly; do not assume permission is granted and provide a graceful fallback when it is denied. Third, device tokens are the identifiers your server uses to target devices; obtain them with getExpoPushTokenAsync or FCM calls, send them securely to your backend, and design server logic to refresh or remove invalid tokens. These three concepts form the backbone of reliable notification delivery and respectful user experience.
